corrections.source_says: The manuscript omits the allocation mechanism, but its linked experimental materials establish it: set Study 1 randomized="yes" and design_class="online_rct". Qualtrics flow FL_133 randomly selects one of three param_condition values, with EvenPresentation=true: active_feedback, active_control, or passive_control. The practice and test branches implement continuous GPT-3 feedback, practice-only feedback, and no feedback, respectively. This is distinct from the separate task-order randomizer FL_64. Update the allocation descriptions and set has_randomized_people_study=true for two-screener routing. Any remaining core-eligibility uncertainty concerns the scope of numerical-only GPT-3 assistance, not random assignment; Study 2 remains a randomized non-generative scoring intervention.

Keep participant exclusions distinct from removed ideas and trials. The manuscript reports 629 recruited and 554 retained, but does not explain overlaps among exclusion categories; do not sum the categories into a separately reported unique participant-exclusion count.

confirmed: Read the complete markdown conversion, including all supplementary text, Tables S1-S9, and supplementary references; checked the underlying 52-page PDF. The title, authors, preprint status, and included supplement match the form (PDF pp. 1, 39-52). No manuscript version number or version date is printed.

The paper-linked Study 1 survey was also read in memory: qualtrics_experiment.qsf, OSF file version 1, https://osf.io/6k52d/files/osfstorage/67534e886ee23eda9c3c1035. Condition randomizer FL_133 selects one feedback condition; task-order randomizer FL_64 separately orders the design problems. This external material supplies the missing random-assignment evidence.

Study 1 used fine-tuned GPT-3 davinci-002 to give numerical originality feedback on human-written design solutions, with continuous, practice-only, and no-feedback arms; practice-only test performance is an after_ai outcome (PDF pp. 9-11; p. 31, lines 644-647; p. 40, Supporting text).

Study 1 analyzed 554 people contributing 7,174 valid responses; these are distinct people and output counts, and the experiment is above the 50-person threshold (PDF p. 16, lines 290-304). Recruitment was through Prolific in the United States, Canada, and United Kingdom (PDF p. 8, lines 121-127).

The Study 1 count conflicts identified by the form are real: 629 recruited on PDF p. 8 versus arm entries of 208, 214, and 208 on p. 11; p. 16 reports 327 engineers and 228 non-engineers, with inconsistent arm totals, whereas Table S1 gives 327 and 227 (PDF p. 43). Retain null for unresolved arm counts and the exact number randomized; the survey randomizer supplies no participant counts.

Study 2 explicitly randomly assigned 18,998 people to immediate feedback and 18,825 to delayed feedback, with 37,823 participants reported before cleaning (PDF pp. 12, 14, lines 209-211 and 249-263). It is a field experiment at a Polish science museum (PDF pp. 12-14).

Study 2 retained 36,198 people: 18,136 immediate-feedback and 18,062 delayed-feedback participants, who provided 77,142 drawings (PDF p. 16, lines 295-301). These counts are not interchangeable, and this experiment is also above the 50-person threshold.

The Study 2 focal contrast concerns the second drawing, following feedback only in the immediate arm. Analyses were restricted to the first two drawings per shape, so the overall drawing count should not be represented as a confirmed count of second-drawing observations (PDF p. 17, lines 319-327).

AuDrA is identified as a convolutional neural network, and only originality scores are supplied to participants. Study 2 alone does not establish generative-AI assistance; the conflicting Methods reference to a large language model is accurately flagged by the form (PDF pp. 6, 13, 29, 31).

Both studies analyze originality at the response level, with participant and prompt random intercepts, rather than participant-aggregated originality (PDF p. 18, lines 339-342; Tables S3 and S6, PDF pp. 45, 48).

Every numerical component of S1-O1 and S1-O2 reported strings matches the PDF, including the means, standard errors, confidence intervals, t statistics, and p values: continuous EMM 6.67 versus control 6.13, d = -0.35; practice-only EMM 6.80 versus control 6.13, d = -0.43. Negative signs are printed in the source despite feedback-favoring arm means (PDF p. 22, lines 432-438).

Every numerical component of S2-O1 reported matches the PDF: second-drawing EMM 4.84 versus 4.44; t(54,419) = -11.83, p < .001; d = -0.20, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.24, -0.17], with both arm SEs and confidence intervals also matching (PDF p. 24, lines 482-485).
The numerical comparisons in one_line_finding match PDF pp. 22 and 24. Its description of Study 1 assignment needs the external-survey qualification recorded above.

This is an original two-study experiment paper, not a synthesis or AI-versus-human output comparison. context_class="none" is appropriate; no pooled synthesis estimates or across-person diversity outcomes are reported (Methods, PDF pp. 8-14; Results, pp. 15-28; supplementary materials, pp. 39-52).

The manuscript explicitly provides materials, data, and analysis scripts at https://osf.io/6k52d/ (PDF pp. 2, 15). The checker accessed its public API and Study 1 survey without saving additional files.
summary: Linked Qualtrics materials confirm that Study 1 randomly assigned people to GPT-3 originality feedback, so it belongs in the two-screener pipeline, with numerical-only assistance flagged for scope review. Reported effect statistics and headline participant counts match the PDF, but design/provenance, preregistration statuses, and exclusion details need correction.
